title: Kippers with Butter
subtitle: Cold-smoked herring jugged in hot water, the British way
excerpt: Kippers cooked by jugging, pouring boiling water over them and leaving them to stand, come out tender and deeply savoury without filling the kitchen with smoke. A knob of butter melting over the top is all they need.
sourceNotes: Jugging kippers is a Victorian method documented by Mrs Beeton and widely used in British households to avoid the pervasive smell of frying smoked fish. The technique appears in editions of Beeton's Book of Household Management from the 1860s onward.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cooking method where food, usually kippers, is placed in a tall container and covered with boiling water, then left to stand off the heat for several minutes. The residual heat cooks the fish gently without direct flame, and avoids the strong smell produced by frying smoked fish.

content.text: Kippers, cold-smoked whole herrings split open and dried, are one of the oldest British breakfast foods, and one of the most misunderstood. Cooked by

, they come out tender and deeply savoury without any of the aggressive smoke smell that puts people off frying them. The method could not be simpler: boiling water, a pan, five minutes of standing, and a knob of {{unsalted-butter}} butter melting over the top.

The kipper has been a British breakfast staple since the mid-nineteenth century. The curing method, splitting a herring and cold-smoking it over oak, is generally credited to John Woodger of Seahouses in Northumberland, around 1843. Similar techniques were used in Scotland and the Isle of Man before that. The Victorian cookery writer Mrs Beeton recommended jugging as the best domestic method in her Book of Household Management. The technique became standard in British homes because it produced good results with no fuss and no lasting smell in the kitchen. Kippers from Craster in Northumberland and Loch Fyne in Scotland are still regarded as the best available.

Bring a full kettle to the boil. Place the {{kippers}} kippers tail-up in a deep saucepan, they should fit snugly. Pour boiling water over them until they are fully submerged, then put a lid on the pan and leave for five minutes. The water does not go back on the heat; the standing temperature is enough to cook the fish all the way through. After five minutes, lift the kippers out carefully with a fish slice, skin-side down, and place them on warm plates. Lay a piece of {{unsalted-butter}} butter over each fish and let it melt into the flesh. Serve with wedges of {{lemon}} lemon and thick brown toast.

Grilling gives a slightly firmer texture and a more pronounced smoky flavour, at the cost of smell. Lay the kippers skin-side up on a baking tray under a hot grill for three to four minutes, you do not need to turn them. The skin becomes lightly crisp and the flesh underneath stays moist from its own oil. Dot with butter to finish. This is the better method if you have good ventilation and want a crisper result. Jugging is the better choice for a flat or poorly ventilated kitchen.

Kippers go with very little. Thick brown toast to soak up the butter and fish juices, a squeeze of lemon, and a pot of tea are the traditional accompaniments. Some people eat them with a soft-boiled egg alongside. The bones are small and numerous, run a fork along the backbone from head to tail to lift most of them, though some will remain. Eating kippers is an occasion rather than a quick breakfast: it is a weekend food, best eaten slowly.

Fish is not cooked through after five minutes: the water was not at a full boil when it went in, or the pan was too large and the water cooled too quickly. Use freshly boiled water and a pan that fits the kippers snugly so the water stays hot.

Kippers are very salty: this is the nature of the cure. A squeeze of lemon cuts through the salt considerably. If they are unpleasantly salty, they may be a lower-quality smoked product, look for traditionally-cured kippers from a fishmonger rather than vacuum-packed supermarket versions.
